name: Salamah ibn al-Khurshub
bio: Salamah ibn al-Khurshub belonged to the Anmar, a stock celebrated, Lyall says, for producing men of mark. Lyall notes difficulties in the genealogy that connects him with the battle of ar-Raqam and doubts whether the first poem is rightly ascribed to him.
Ode V is addressed to 'Amir ibn at-Tufail; Ode VI, from verse 3 onward, praises his mare.

poems.title: Ode V: When ye go forth in the
poems.author: Salamah ibn al-Khurshub
poems.note: Lyall's heading: Salamah son of al-Khurshub, of Anmar.
poems.text:
When ye go forth in the morning making for our land again, ye Sons of 'Amir, stock yourselves well with hangman's ropes !

The Sons of Dhubyan — know it well ! — are still where ye found them the last time, in the bend of the valley of al-Batll, some pasturing in the wilderness, some settled in villages ;

They block the doors of the lordly tents with well-trained steeds, tethered by head-ropes to penfolds [containing she-camels set apart to yield them milk].

A mighty concourse are they : no stranger breaks their unity of stock at all the waters between Faid and Sajir ;

Their gatherers of firewood go far away until they reach the woods of tamarisk that overhang the barren sands.

Thou didst escape with a blade that had no scabbard on it, and a saddle that was too short to fit the back of ar-Eihalah :

So praise her well for her service to thee, as is fitting, and be not ungrateful to her — the ungrateful has no prosperity !

Had she been galloping on the ground, she had been overtaken : but she flew through the air with thee like an eagle

Dusky of hue, with supple wings, whose feathers have been matted together by the rain of a day of heavy and frequent showers.

May every one in the tribe that falls short of his purpose, whether a seeker after vengeance or the inflicter of a blow, be a sacrifice for Abu Asma !

Thou hast given in thy bounty camels of full age that have just conceived, then those in the tenth month of pregnancy ; and thou hast not withheld even the she-camel that yields, at a milking, a row of bowls, appointed as a nurse for the calves of others.

He pairs his steeds [for the foray] with riding camels, and they outstrip all others in the hurried advance, braving the heat of the noon-day ;

Then overtook the enemy in the east of al-Maraurat in the afternoon the remnant of the offspring of al-Quraqir ;

And there escaped not of them any save [those that had] mares with deep-sunken eyes, that claim to be of noble stock by their long necks, like the stallion-camel that challenges and beats all his rivals.

At Sahuq they poured forth on the ground many hospitable bowls, and they made over [to our tribe as booty] others, some full of milk set apart to curdle, and some of milk already sour.

Yea and thou, O 'Amir son of the Rider of Qurzul, again thou fallest back upon vile and unseemly speech !

poems.title: Ode VI: There comes to him time after
poems.author: Salamah ibn al-Khurshub
poems.text:
There comes to him time after time the nightly vision of Sulaima, even as the creditor besets with his importunities his debtor.

If she brings with her that which she knows [i. e. her love in exchange for mine] — then verily — God be praised ! — I am one who can give love for love, and also one who can cut the bond if love wanes.

Yea, many the meadow through which one wades [as through a pool], wherein the dust-coloured [ostriches] lay their eggs — the greenery of it has been forbidden to men, and the growth is lush and high —

Have I visited in the morning, carried hither and thither by a swimming mare, the splinters of the frogs of whose hoofs are as hard as date-stones fully ripe:

One of those mares that look about them on this side and that [through sprightliness], what time the sweat has soaked the saddle-girth.

When the girth [under stress of galloping] slips back to a place just in front of her short ribs, the place where a woman's girdle goes round her waist,

Sometimes it strikes against the points of her teats, and sometimes the galloping brings it back to its proper place and it is straight again.

She is a bay, of no doubtful hue, but the colour of sirf into which the hide to be dyed has been plunged a second time.

Three of her legs are like one another in having a white ring round the pastern, while one leg is all of one colour.

It seems as though on them [the three legs] were bands of purest silver, such as that from which are made earrings uplifted by a dainty ear.

She is shielded by charms so that she takes no hurt [from an evil eye], and amulets are tied on to her neck-gear.

And when we go hunting, she puts within our power the loudly-braying wild-ass, whom the lush herbage has made as strong as a demon,

With the swoop of an eagle of 'Ardah which has been stirred by the sight, in Dhu-d-Dumran, of a hare that trips with short steps.
